title: Is Node.js is a language or framework?

content.text: Node.js is not a language or a framework, but rather a JavaScript Runtime Environment that allows developers to run JavaScript outside the browser.
Open source, server-side JavaScript runtime.
Allows you to run JavaScript on your machine or on servers.
Built on the V8 JavaScript engine for speed.
Robust ecosystem with npm.
Node is all about Modules.
Open-Source means that the source code of Node.js is publicly available.

content.type: Anyone can:

content.text: View: You can see how Node.js is built under the hood.
Modify: If you want to customize or improve Node.js, you can do it.
Contribute: Developers around the world actively contribute to improve Node.js.
Cross Platform means Node.js can run on multiple operating systems without needing major changes.

content.type: Supported Platforms:
content.text: Windows, MacOS, Linux
JavaScript Runtime Environment refers to the environment where your JavaScript code runs.

content.type: In Browsers:
content.text: JavaScript typically runs in the browser (like Chrome or Firefox) to handle frontend tasks.

content.type: With Node.js:
content.text: Node.js allows JavaScript to run outside the browser, on the server.
It provides tools to interact with the server, like:
File system (read/write files)
Network (handles HTTP requests)
Database (connect to database like MongoDB or MySQL)

title: Why Node.js Special as a Runtime?

content.type: ▪ V8 Engine:
content.text: Node.js uses Google Chrome V8 Engine to compile JavaScript into machine code, making it lightning fast.

content.type: ▪ Built-int APIs:
content.text: Node.js comes with Built-in APIs (like fs for file systems or http for servers) so you can build powerful applications without extra libraries.
Single Language for Full Stack Development:
Developers can use JavaScript for both frontend and backend, reducing complexity.
For example, a MERN Stack Project (like MongoDB, Express, React, Node).
High Performance:
Thanks, to the V8 engine, Node.js is super fast.
It can handle thousands of simultaneous connection with ease.
Event-Driven and Non-Blocking I/O:
Unlike traditional servers that block a thread for each request, Node.js uses an asynchronous model, making it highly efficient for handling multiple tasks.
Scalable for modern applications:
Ideal for real-time applications like chat apps, streaming platforms or online games.
It stands for Read-Eval-Print Loop or Read, Evaluate, Print and Loop. It's an interactive programming environment that allows you to execute JavaScript code one statement at a time.
You can open your terminal and use node command.
You can use it to taste simple JavaScript code similar to browser devtools.
CRTL + C to exit out of it.
Each part of the acronym highlights a specific step in how the REPL works:
Read: The REPL read the user's input (a single line or multiple line of code) and parses it to a data structure that JavaScript engine can understand.
Eval (Evaluate): The parsed input is evaluated (executed) by JavaScript engine. If the input is a valid expression, the REPL computes the result.
Print: The result of the evaluated expression is printed on the console so the user can see the output.
Loop: The process then loops back, waiting for the input, and continues until the user exits.
In Node.js there is no window or document. Why? Because Node.js runs outside the browser - it doesn't deal with the DOM or browser-specific APIs.
Instead, Node.js has a global object. It's the equivalent of window in the browser but designed for a server-side environment.
globalThis is a new feature introduced in ECMAScript 2020 (ES11) that provides a standard way to access the global object in any JavaScript environment.
What is it useful?

content.type: Consistent Access:
content.text: In the past, accessing the global object varied depending on the environment:
Browser: window
Node.js: global
Web Workers: self
Other Environments: Might have there own global objects
Self-contained code unit:
Each file in a Noe.js is treated as a separate file.
Variables, functions or objects defined in one file are not accessible by another file by default unless you explicitly export them.

content.type: 2. Encapsulation:

content.text: Node.js uses the commons module system (module.exports for export and require for import) to ensure the code in one file does not pollute or interfere with the global scope.
This makes your code modular, maintainable and easier to debug.

content.type: // math.js
const add = (a, b) => a + b;
module.exports = add;
// app.js
const add = require('./math');
content.text: console.log(add(5, 10));      // Output: 15

title: Named and Aggregate Exports and Imports.

content.text: Avoid mixing module.exports and exports.property incorrectly. If you reassign module.exports, it will override any exports.property assignment.
Use consistent syntax for clarity:
Assign everything at once with module.exports = {...};
Eg: module.exports = {add, sub, multi, div};
Or assign properties individually with module.exports.property.
Eg: module.exports.add; module.exports.sub; modules.exports.multi;
Also while import:
Assign everything at once like const {...} = require('./math');
Or assign in a variable like const math = require('./math') and use method to apply the function.
Eg: const {add, sub, multi, div} = require('./math');
Eg: const math = require('./math'); // math.add, math.sub, math.multi, math.div
In Node.js, path module provides utilities for working with file and directory paths. It's a built-in module, so you don't need to install any external package to use it.

content.type: const path = require('path');
Special Node.js Constants:
1. __filename:
content.text: Provide the absolute path of the currently executing file.

content.type: 2. __dirname:
content.text: Provide absolute directory path of the currently executing file.

content.type: 1. path.parse():
content.text: Return an object with details about the given path, including root, dir, name, ext and base.

content.type: 2. path.join():
content.text: Joins multiple path segments into one, using the appropriate separator.

content.type: 3. path.resolve():
content.text: Resolve a sequence of into an absolute path, starting from the current directory.

content.type: 4. path.extname():
content.text: Extracts a file extension from a given path.

content.type: 5. path.basename():
content.text: Returns the last part of the path. (eg. file name with extension)

content.type: 6. path.dirname():
content.text: Returns a directory part of a path.

content.type: 7. path.sep:
content.text: Returns the platform specific path segment separator.

The fs (File System) module in Node.js is a core module that allows you to work with the file system, enabling you to read, write, update, delete, and watch files.

content.type: 1. Create:
content.text: Writes content to the file. If the file does not exist, it creates one.
Syntax: fs.writeFileSync(filePath, data, options)

content.type: 2. Read:
content.text: Reads the content of the file asynchronously and logs it.
Syntax: const data = fs.readFileSync(filePath, options)

content.type: 3. Update:
content.text: Appends new content to the file without overwriting the existing content.
Syntax: fs.appendFileSync(filePath, data, options)

content.type: 4. Delete:
content.text: Deletes the file completely.
Syntax: fs.unlinkSync(filePath)

content.type: 5. Rename:
content.text: Renames a file from one name to another.
Syntax: fs.renameSync(oldPath, newPath)

content.type: 1. Create:
content.text: Writes data to a file, replacing the file if it already exists.
Syntax: fs.writeFile(path, data, options, callback)

content.type: 2. Read:
content.text: Reads the contents of a file asynchronously and returns the data as a buffer or string.
Syntax: fs.readFile(path, options, callback)

content.type: 3. Update:
content.text: Appends data to a file. If the file doesn’t exist, it is created.
Syntax: fs.appendFile(path, data, options, callback)

content.type: 4. Delete:
content.text: Deletes a file asynchronously.
Syntax: fs.unlink(path, callback)

content.type: 5. Rename:
content.text: Rename a file asynchronously.
Syntax: fs.unlink(oldPath, newPath, callback)

content.type: Example:
1. Create:
content.text: Creates or overwrites a file with specified content.
Syntax: fs.promises.writeFile(path, data, options).then('File created.').catch()

content.type: 2. Read:
content.text: The readFile() method reads data from a file.
Syntax: fs.promises.readFile(path, options).then((data) => console.log(data)).catch((err) => console.error(err))

content.type: 3. Update:
content.text: The appendFile() method adds content without overwriting the existing data.
syntax: fs.promises.appendFile(path, data, options).then('File updated.').catch()

content.type: 4. Delete:
content.text: The unlink() method removes the specified file asynchronously.
Syntax: fs.promises.unlink(path).then().catch()

title: FS Module using Async Await Promises way.

content.type: 1. Create:
content.text: Writes data to a file asynchronously. If the file exists, it overwrites the content.
Syntax: fs.Promises.writeFile(path, data, options)

content.type: 2. Read:
content.text: Reads the contents of a file asynchronously.
Syntax: fsPromises.readFile(path, options)

content.type: 3. Update:
content.text: Adds content to the end of a file. If the file does not exist, it creates a new one.
Syntax: fsPromises.appendFile(path, data, options)

content.type: 4. Delete:
content.text: Deletes a file by its path.
Syntax: fsPromises.unlink(path)

title: Advantages and Use Cases of FS Module.

content.type: Advantages:

content.text: No need for manual callbacks.
Cleaner and more intuitive asynchronous workflows using async/await.
Suitable for modern JavaScript applications.

content.type: Use Cases:

content.text: Reading Files asynchronously in a non-blocking way.
Writing or Appending Data to files without blocking the event loop.
Performing Multiple File Operations sequentially or concurrently with promise chaining.
Handling Errors Gracefully with .catch() or try...catch blocks.

▪ Streams in Node.js are a way to handle continuous flow of data.
▪ They enable reading or writing data piece by piece instead of loading the entire data into memory.
▪ A Buffer in Node.js is a temporary storage area for binary data.
▪ Buffers work as chunks of data, enabling efficient data manipulation in streams.
▪ It helps to decrease memory consumption of your web server.
▪ There are four types of streams in Node.js: Writeable, Readable, Duplex, and Transform.

▪ The http module in Node.js allows developers to create an HTTP server and handle client requests and server responses. It provides methods and properties to work with HTTP requests and responses, enabling the creation of REST APIs, web pages, and other networked applications.

▪ A web server is software or hardware that serves web content (HTML, CSS, JavaScript, etc.) to clients (usually browsers) over the internet or an intranet. It uses protocols like HTTP/HTTPS to handle requests and responses.
Step 1: Importing the http Module
▪ The http module is built into Node.js. Use require('http') to import it into your script.
Step 2: Using http.createServer()
▪ The createServer method initializes an HTTP server.
▪ It takes a callback function as an argument with two parameters:
a. req: the incoming request object.
b. res: the outgoing response object.
Step 3: Handling Requests
▪ The req.url property provides the path requested by the client.
▪ Based on req.url, send different responses using res.end().
Step 4: Starting the Server
▪ Use the listen() method to specify the port the server will run on.
▪ Optionally, pass a callback to run code when the server starts (e.g., console.log()).

▪ HTTPS is the secure version of HTTP, using SSL/TLS encryption to protect data during transmission.
▪ The browser send HTTP/HTTPS request to the server for a specific resource (e.g., webpage, image).
▪ There are different types of HTTP methods like GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH, etc.

▪ Route parameters in Express.js are dynamic parts of URL that can be accessed using req.params.
▪ They are defined in the route path with colon(:), eg., user/:id/view/:article where id is a route parameter.
▪ You can access the value of route parameter via req.params.id, req.params.article in the route handler.
▪ Route parameters are used to capture values from the URL and pass them to the route handler for processing, like user IDs, product names, etc.
▪ Express automatically parses and makes the value available in req.params as object where the parameter name is the key.
▪ Query parameters are key-value pairs appended to a URL after '?', separated by '&', like '/product?search=mobile&limit=10'.
▪ In Express.js, they can be accessed using req.query, which returns an object containing the parameters.
▪ For example, in '/search?page=4', req.query.page will give you page number.
▪ Query parameters are often used to pass optional or filter data to the server without modifying the route.
▪ They are always part of the URL and visible in browser address bar.
▪ You can use the <form> tag with the action attribute to specify the URL to which the form data is submitted.
▪ Example: <form action='/contact' method='post'>
▪ By default, the form will use GET request, and you handle it with app.get to access form data by req.query, as the data is sent through the URL as query strings.
▪ Since URLs have the length limits, you can use the POST method for form submissions, which send the data in the request body, allowing for larger amounts of data.
▪ To access data from a POST request, use must first use the express.urlencoded() middleware to parse the request body.
▪ Example: app.use(express.urlencoded({ extended: true }));
▪ The urlencoded option { extended: true } uses the qs library to parse the query string, allowing for more complex structures like nested objects, which the default parser cannot handle.
▪ Use req.body in app.post to access the form data send in the body of POST request.
▪ Example: console.log(req.body);
▪ Use a middleware function with no specific route, like app.use((req, res) => {...}), to handle unmatched routes.
▪ Example: return res.status(404).send('Page Not Found!'));
▪ Inside the middleware, send a 404 status using res.status(404) and a custom message or HTML response.
▪ Place this middleware after all defined routes to catch only unhandled requests.
▪ Example: app.use((req, res) => { return res.status(404).send('Page Not Found!'));});
▪ Example: app.use((req, res) => { return res.status(404).sendFile(path.join(import.meta.dirname, 'views', '404.html'));});
▪ A router in Express.js is a tool to define modular and reusable routes in an application.
▪ It is created using express.Router() to handle related routes together.
▪ Routes can be defined using methods like router.get() or router.post().
▪ The router is mounted in the main app using app.use('/base_path', router).
▪ Syntax:
import { Router } from 'express';
const router = Router();
▪ A templet engine in Express.js is used to render dynamic HTML by injecting data into templets.
▪ Popular engines like EJS, Pug or Handlebars can be integrated with Express.
▪ All engines have different syntax similar to HTML, but it helps to pass down dynamic values from express to HTML.
▪ Set the engine using app.set('view engine', 'ejs') and specify the template folder with app.set('views', './views').
▪ Render templates using res.render('templateName', {key: value}).
▪ res.render('index', {title: 'Welcome', message: 'Hello World!'});
▪ Install the engine using npm (eg. npm install ejs) and create templates using placeholders like <%=title %> for data insertion.
▪ EJS (Embedded JavaScript) is a simple templating engine for generating dynamic HTML pages.
▪ It integrates JavaScript logic into HTML using specific tags like <%= %>.
▪ Support JavaScript features like loops, conditionals and partials.
▪ Escapes HTML by default to prevent injection, with options for unescaped output.
▪ Widely used with Express.js for rendering views dynamically.
▪ Re-use common templates like headers, footers, etc., using include.
▪ Example:
<%- include('header') %>

▪ MVC is a software design pattern that separates an application into 3 distinct layers: Model, View and Controller, each with specific responsibilities.
▪ Model: Manages Data and Logic Represents the data of the application, handles business logic, and interacts with the database (e.g., CRUD Operations).
▪ View: Handles User Interface Displays the data to the user. It's responsible for rendering the presentations (HTML, CSS, JavaScript) based on the data provided by the controller.
▪ Controller: The Mediator Acts as the intermediary between the Model and View. It handles user input, interacts with the Model to fetch or update data, and passes the data to the View for display.
Model (Warehouse):
▪ Model represents the data and logic to handle it. Think of it as a warehouse where all the goods (data) are stored.
▪ It's responsible for managing and updating data.
View (Shop or Customer):
▪ View is the final interface where the customer interacts.
▪ It could be the shop displaying products (e.g., HTML, CSS on a webpage) or the person who ordered or who sees the delivered product.
▪ The view only knows how to present the data but doesn't handle or process it directly.
Controller (Delivery Person):
▪ Controller is the middle man or the mediator like the delivery boy. Example:
▪ Gets the order from the customer (View)..
▪ Fetches the right product (Data) from the warehouse (Model).
▪ Delivers the goods back to customer (View)
▪ A database is a structured way to store and manage data.
▪ It helps organize data for easy access, retrieval and updates.
▪ Databases store data like tables, documents, and key-value pairs.
▪ They are used in applications to handle user and system data.
▪ Databases ensure data is consistent and available when needed.
▪ Examples include MySQL, PostgreSQL, MongoDB and Redis.
▪ Data Integrity: Ensures data consistency. For example, in banking, a transaction is either happens fully or not at all.
▪ Concurrency Management: Discuss how multiple users can access the same data simultaneously without conflicts.
▪ Backup & Recovery: Automatics processes to save data and restore it after failures.
▪ Scalability: Mention how databases are designed to handle growth from hundreds to millions of records.
